Spring, TX Considerations

Spring has the usual Houston-area clay problems, plus some that are more specific to it: ground sinking, creek flooding, heavy tree cover and older subdivisions.

Spring, TX Characteristics

Clay under sandy loam

North Harris County soil is sandy loam over expansive clay. The clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, and the mix can change from one street to the next.

Watch for: Cracks that open in summer and close after rain

A high water table

Neighborhoods near Spring Creek and Cypress Creek sit on flat ground with shallow groundwater, so drainage is often part of the repair.

Watch for: Soggy yard spots or water standing by the slab

Ground subsidence

Decades of groundwater pumping in north Harris and south Montgomery counties have caused the land to sink in places, adding slow movement under slabs.

Watch for: Slow, steady cracking over years with no clear cause

Heavy rain and flooding

Gulf storms can drop inches of rain in a day. Saturated soil followed by long dry spells is hard on any foundation.

Watch for: Doors and windows that stick after a big storm

Big trees close to the house

Mature oaks and pines pull moisture from the soil around the slab, which leads to settlement on the side nearest the roots.

Watch for: Cracks and low floors on the side closest to the tree
★WHAT'S HAPPENING IN SPRING

Local Issues Affecting Spring Foundations

Sinking ground, faults, droughts, storms and floods all play a part in how Spring foundations move. Here is what is happening locally and what it means for your home.

SUBSIDENCE

Spring is sinking, slowly

Harris-Galveston Subsidence District GPS stations show north Spring sinking about 1.6 to 1.9 cm a year. The station near I-45 and the Grand Parkway is down about 31 cm over 18 years.
Spring has sunk about 4.2 feet on average since 1906, and roughly 70% of north Harris County water still comes from groundwater.
Subsidence is regional. Its biggest effect on homes is worse drainage and flooding, not cracks in a single slab.
FAULT LINES

Growth faults in north Harris County

The Houston area has about 300 known faults. USGS reports many move 0.5 to 2 cm a year and have damaged hundreds of structures.
Buying a home? Check the fault map before you close.
DROUGHT & RAIN

Drought, then heavy rain

The 2011, 2022 and 2023 droughts all brought surges of foundation calls across the Houston area.
In 2023, Houston leak calls hit about 500 a week, up from about 300 the year before, as shifting soil broke pipes.
When rain returns after a drought, the clay swells and a second wave of movement follows.
STORMS & TREES

Storms and falling trees

The May 2024 storms and Hurricane Beryl in July 2024 dropped trees onto homes across Spring, including Timber Lane and River Plantation.
When a big tree comes down near the house, its roots and stump can disturb the soil under the slab. Get an inspection after the cleanup.
FLOODING

Spring Creek and Cypress Creek flooding

Hurricane Harvey flooded about 9,450 homes in the Cypress Creek watershed.
Older subdivisions built in the 1960s to 80s, such as Champion Forest, Ponderosa Forest and Westador, are among the most flood-prone. The county flood control district has bought out more than 150 homes in Spring and Klein.
Water that sits under and around a slab softens the soil. Check your foundation after any flood.
NEW BUILDS

Cracks in a newer home

The Grand Parkway boom left thousands of 5 to 10 year old builder-grade slabs in the Spring area.
Builders often call early cracks cosmetic. Texas law (RCLA) requires a notice letter to the builder before a lawsuit, and there is a 10-year statute of repose.
An independent elevation survey gives you a record of movement while you are still covered.
★SPRING SOIL TYPE

Spring, TX Soil and What It Does to Foundations

Spring sits on two old Gulf Coast geologic layers. The upper one is expansive clay that swells when wet and shrinks when dry, and it is the main reason foundations here move.

The two layers under Spring

  • ★ Beaumont FormationPlastic, compressible clay and mud laid down in flood basins, coastal lakes and old stream channels. In the Houston area this clay can be up to 40 feet deep. It is the main troublemaker.
  • ★ Lissie FormationOlder and sandier: sand, silt, clay and some gravel, sitting beneath the Beaumont. Both are mapped in Harris and Montgomery counties, Spring's two counties.
  • ★ Why it varies street to streetSpring sits near where the clayey and sandier ground meet, so soil conditions can change over short distances. Two neighboring homes can behave differently.

How expansive is it?

A University of Houston study of Houston-area clays measured:

  • ★ High-plasticity clay (CH)Average liquid limit of 59% and plasticity index (PI) of 34%.
  • ★ Lower-plasticity clay (CL)Average liquid limit of 38% and PI of 20%.
  • ★ What PI meansA higher plasticity index means more swelling and shrinking. A PI over 50 is considered highly plastic and very expansive.
  • ★ The causeExpansive soils contain smectite clay minerals, which absorb water between their layers and change volume.
★COMMON ISSUES

Common Foundation Issues in Spring, TX

Spring has the usual Houston-area clay problems, plus some that are more specific to it: ground sinking, creek flooding, heavy tree cover and older subdivisions.

1. Clay heave and settlement

  • ★ What it isThe slab rises when the clay is wet and drops when it dries. Edges and corners move most.
  • ★ SignsCracks above doors and windows, sticking doors, stair-step cracks in brick, sloping floors.
  • ★ Worst timesAfter a long drought (settlement) or a very wet season (heave).

2. Ground sinking (subsidence)

  • ★ How muchSpring has sunk about 4.2 feet over the past century, more than The Woodlands or Conroe, most of it since 1987.
  • ★ Where it's fastestA University of Houston study found north Spring had some of the fastest sinking in the Houston area from 2016 to 2020, especially near I-45 and the Grand Parkway. A monitoring station off Lindell Road in 77373 has dropped more than 30 cm since 2007.
  • ★ WhyGroundwater pumping. About 70% of water use in northern Harris County comes from groundwater.
  • ★ What it means for homesThe area sinks fairly evenly, so it rarely cracks one house by itself. But it worsens flooding and, over time, can damage pipes, roads and property.

3. Flooding and creek erosion

  • ★ The creeksSpring sits along Cypress Creek and Spring Creek. During Harvey, the Cypress Creek watershed got 29.3 inches of rain and 9,450 homes flooded, including in Inverness Forest and Northwood Pines.
  • ★ Foundation effectsSoil washed out at slab edges, swollen clay followed by sudden drying, and damaged pier and beam crawl spaces.

4. Trees

  • ★ The problemSpring is heavily wooded with pines and oaks, often close to houses. In droughts, roots dry out soil at one edge of the slab.
  • ★ The fixRoot barriers and moisture control.

5. Plumbing leaks under the slab

  • ★ The problemSome Spring homes still have cast-iron plumbing, which corrodes. A leak keeps one area of clay wet, causing heave or washout in that spot.
  • ★ How it's foundA hydrostatic plumbing test.

6. Older subdivisions

  • ★ WhereChampion Forest, Northgate Forest, Inverness Forest and other neighborhoods from the 1970s and 80s.
  • ★ Why it mattersOlder slabs, older plumbing, mature trees, and sometimes earlier repairs that are now failing.

7. Poor drainage

  • ★ The problemFlat lots, overwhelmed street drains and missing gutters let water pool against the slab, especially when heavy rain hits saturated ground.
